ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Meconium aspiration: 3

A newborn with aspirated meconium has poor gas exchange even in regions without complete airway blockage. The team discusses direct inflammatory injury and impaired alveolar surface-tension control. Which mechanism contributes to these problems beyond mechanical plugging?

  1. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
  2. Prioritize effective ventilation; suction only when obstruction warrants it
  3. Chemical pneumonitis with surfactant dysfunction
  4. Meconium aspiration syndrome
  5. Partial airway obstruction with air trapping
Answer and explanation

Chemical pneumonitis with surfactant dysfunction

Meconium injures the lung and disrupts surfactant, contributing to impaired gas exchange and atelectasis.

Option explanations

Chemical pneumonitis with surfactant dysfunction: Meconium injures the lung and disrupts surfactant, contributing to impaired gas exchange and atelectasis.

Meconium aspiration syndrome: Respiratory distress after meconium exposure in a term or post-term infant can reflect aspiration-related lung disease; other causes still require consideration. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Partial airway obstruction with air trapping: A ball-valve effect permits inspiration more readily than expiration, promoting hyperinflation and air leak. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: Persistently high pulmonary vascular resistance can drive right-to-left shunting and worsen hypoxemia in severe neonatal lung disease. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Prioritize effective ventilation; suction only when obstruction warrants it: Routine suction solely for meconium exposure can delay needed ventilation. Obstruction preventing effective ventilation may require airway clearance. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
